Action segmentation is a key step in understanding human behavior, yet existing state-of-the-frame approaches are limited to providing labels for individual frames without modeling temporal relationships between consecutive actions. To bridge this gap, we propose a paradigm called Coordinated Human Movements, which treats each action instance as a directed graph composed of limb actions. We introduce a new dataset, CHMD, featuring graphical representations with limb-level annotations across various activities. We also present a new class of methods called Graphical Action Recognition, which translates graphical representations into actions and their corresponding timestamps. We evaluate the effectiveness of this framework on CHMD and demonstrate that incorporating coordinated human movements significantly aids in action recognition and temporal localization. While many approaches are designed for continuous domains, such as image rotation, they often fail when the domain shift involves discrete variations, like different image augmentations. This paper introduces a new domain adaptation framework specifically for discrete domain adaptation. This framework builds upon the idea of mapping discrete domains into a feature space using a learned kernel matrix, which is then optimized with an objective function tailored to minimize the discrepancy between training and testing domains. Since our approach is domain-agnostic, it can be applied to any task, though we demonstrate it most effectively on text classification. We evaluate the method on text classification tasks, showing that it surpasses state-of-the-time techniques like DKAD and TDA. Furthermore, we extend the method to the broader classification task, and while it does not consistently outperform other methods, it performs competitively against several recent approaches. Finally, we also apply the method to NLP generation tasks, achieving results comparable to, or slightly better than, the state-of-the-art. Overall, our method offers a promising and competitive solution for discrete domain adaptation. The code is available at https://github.com/ashishg/dak. Please cite as follows:

1000 A*V binaries and 1000 spurious doubles, gathered using the 1.5m TACO telescope at the CTIO in Chile, to investigate the impact of source confusion on the identification of spurious doubles. These observations were conducted to determine the frequency of such confusion errors within the larger SpeRBI survey, a significant initiative in exoplanet research. The primary objective is to assess whether these errors affect the reliability of the radial-velocity method for detecting exoplanets. To achieve this, we analyzed the individual components of the observed systems and conducted a statistical analysis of the resulting data. Our findings indicate that the TACO instrument is highly susceptible to source confusion errors, with a probability of approximately 10% for a spurious double to be mistakenly classified as an A*V binary. This error rate is notably higher than rates found in other speckle surveys, primarily due to the greater number of sources in the TACO field of view, which ranges from 100 to over 1000 depending on magnitude. Furthermore, the majority of these confusion errors involve additional stars with V magnitudes less than 16. Finally, we explore potential solutions to mitigate this risk, including the application of statistical methods to distinguish between spurious doubles and genuine binaries. This approach could reduce the error rate to less than 1% if confusion errors are detected. Consequently, we recommend that future projects incorporate simultaneous observations of nearby stars to validate the authenticity of candidates identified by the SpeRBI survey. Additionally, we propose that the data from the already completed observations of these systems be utilized to refine statistical methods for exoplanet detection. In this context, we have developed a new technique to distinguish between confusion errors and real binaries, which will be detailed in a separate paper. Ultimately, this work aims to enhance the understanding of binary star populations and facilitate the discovery of exoplanets within these systems. The research was conducted under the supervision of Dr. José Alvarado. (Abstract abridged)

This study examines a well-documented eruption of a large active region on June 12, 2016, observed by multiple instruments. Raster-scanning imaging of the June 16, 2016 eruption by RHESSI revealed a co-spatial source of hard X-rays (HXR) exhibiting temporal variability indicative of a "cracking" motion within the source. Concurrently, the Reuven Ramaty High Energy Solar Spectroscopic Telescope (RHESSST) detected a geosynchronous gamma-ray emission with a spectrum resembling the "crack" motion seen in HXR imagery. This work presents simultaneous observations of the eruption's coronal mass ejection (CME) and associated HXR emissions across various energies using the Imaging Atmospheric Cherenkov Telescope (IACT) array. The findings indicate that the CME's shock front, traveling at approximately 1000 km/s, generated chorus emissions detectable by the IACT. These results suggest that the CME shock front likely accelerated both electrons and protons. The detection of emissions across multiple instruments with differing energy sensitivities offers valuable insights into the physical mechanisms of particle acceleration driven by CME shocks. Ultimately, this work underscores the value of multi-instrumental observations for understanding the processes occurring within solar eruptions. (Abstract abridged).

Magnetic field lines spiral around the toroid while oscillating between the poles, enabling ions and electrons to maintain gyro-orbits around these lines without traversing across them. The proposed system is envisioned as a compact, closed plasma containment structure with broad applications, including the observation of magnetic reconnection and electron runaway phenomena. To investigate the system's physical properties, numerical simulations were conducted using Particle-in-Cell (PIC) software. These simulations employed parameters derived from a proposed laboratory-scale configuration, featuring a magnetic field strength of approximately 0.05 Tesla, a toroid radius of roughly 0.5 meters, and an oblateness of 0.8. The plasma was composed of deuterium with an electron temperature of 1 eV and a density of $10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$. Results indicate that the configuration is stable, with ions and electrons effectively confined within the toroidal cavity. Notably, no particles escaped through the magnetic mirrors at the poles. Furthermore, the study observed that runaway electrons generated via triangle collisions remained confined inside the toroid. These findings suggest the potential for plasma magnetic mirrors to serve as a containment mechanism in closed 3D systems. Additionally, the research explored the potential for self-organization within this configuration. Future investigations should aim to examine the specific conditions required to achieve such organization. Ultimately, this work opens new avenues for research into the physical phenomena this configuration may facilitate.

This paper presents a novel off-policy value function estimator tailored for Markov decision processes with continuous state and action spaces. The study addresses the associated parabolic initial-boundary value problem, focusing on the relationship between weak and strong solutions and the corresponding strong parabolic equation. The analysis establishes conditions under which the existence of a strong solution guarantees the presence of a weak solution, with the primary focus on LLT-type equations. The methodology relies on a technique by Kim and Naddaf, which  connects the existence of weak solutions to the existence of the fundamental solution and its heat estimates,  combined with the construction of Doob's h-transform and its subsequent estimation. The primary innovation lies in the use of alternative, more robust estimates for the h-transform and fundamental solution, derived from the specific structure of the perturbation, to derive the existence of weak solutions, alongside the previously cited technique by Kim and Naddaf. The work addresses scenarios where the secondary term is neither a Drift-Zhang nor a singular potential. As an application, the paper investigates the relative size of the weak existence threshold for elliptic-LLT operators featuring degenerate or singular main terms and Drift-Zhang or non-singular Weyl-type lower-order terms, which are known to lie at the boundary of this critical line. Additionally, the study analyzes the case where the lower-order term is a Drift-Kato potential, which falls below the critical threshold. In both applications, the analysis of the h-transform is significantly more intricate due to the Drift-Zhang nature of the operator. The paper concludes by discussing Dirichlet problems, highlighting the distinct differences in methodology and the resulting results. Finally, the weak existence criterion for the Dirichlet problem is compared, and the influence of the boundary condition on the lower-order term is analyzed. It offers an alternative approach to existing methodologies, demonstrating that h-transforms provide a more natural framework for this class of equations. While the current work concentrates on the degenerate case, future efforts will address scenarios where the lower-order term exhibits growth at infinity. While prior research has developed quantization-based methods to enhance privacy and reduce costs, these approaches often suffer from decreased communication efficiency and increased training time due to the necessity of multiple iterations per update. To address this, we propose a privacy-preserving communication efficiency improvement (PCEI) method that leverages large-scale pre-training. This method is designed for scenarios where sufficient pre-trained models are available for most participants, allowing the model to adapt to specific tasks while maintaining privacy and minimizing communication overhead. We demonstrate that the F-LAMP algorithm, a recent large-scale linear adaptation technique, is suitable for this PCEI approach and can effectively balance privacy and communication efficiency. Furthermore, we extend the method to cover a broader range of tasks, such as image classification, by employing non-linear large-scale adaptation techniques. Experimental results across various tasks show that our method not only safeguards participant privacy but also improves communication efficiency by up to 99%. Additionally, we analyze the impact of the number of participants and the size of the pre-trained model. Finally, we evaluate the method's robustness against adversarial attacks, confirming its practical applicability. To our knowledge, this is the first study to explore the alignment between large-scale pre-training and privacy-efficient training methods for federated learning. We have made our code and experiments public to facilitate further research. The public access link is: https://github.com/zhengruif/fpcei. We hope this resource will be valuable to the community. Our analysis reveals that the FUV spectrum exhibits significant features arising from carbon-rich molecules, including CN, $a^3\Pi$ $C_2$, $X^1\Sigma_g^+$ N$_2$,$a^3\Pi_g$ C$_2$, and $X^1\Sigma_g^+$ CN. The relative intensities of these molecular features indicate that the FUV spectrum is dominated by emission from the dense inner circumstellar region, with a contribution from the densest zones peaking at a radius of approximately 10$^{-3}$ pc. The cumulative effect of these intense FUV features is that the continuum emission peaks at wavelengths of 1200 $\AA$ and 1250 $\AA$, rather than at 1100 $\AA$ as typically observed in other carbon-rich stars. This shift occurs because the strong features cause a substantial drop in flux at wavelengths exceeding 1200 $\AA$. We attribute this unusual spectral behavior to the presence of a dense, carbon-rich inner wind around IRC+10216. Furthermore, we demonstrate that including molecular features in model atmospheres for stars like IRC+10216 can account for the observed discrepancy between the stellar effective temperature and the dust condensation temperature. Finally, we highlight that the intense FUV features in IRC+10216 could potentially explain its high mass-loss rate. These characteristics make IRC+10216 a valuable probe for investigating the initial stages of mass loss in evolved stars. Additionally, the distinctive shape of its FUV spectrum provides a benchmark for refining the chemistry of carbon-rich environments, which is essential for utilizing future space-based FUV/UV spectrographs. A key finding in this domain is that networks with modular structures, where nodes cluster into distinct communities, are more resilient to random node failures. In a recently published study, we extend this conclusion to scenarios involving targeted attacks, which involve the strategic removal of nodes to compromise stability. Specifically, our findings demonstrate that networks with modular architectures require the removal of far more nodes to reach an unstable state compared to non-modular networks. Furthermore, we establish that modularity is a critical determinant of stability, potentially serving as a foundational principle in various fields, including neuroscience, ecology, and social network analysis. However, it is important to note that while modularity generally enhances stability, there are specific parameter regimes where this effect is negligible. Ultimately, by delineating the conditions under which modularity enhances stability, our research offers a deeper understanding of the fundamental properties governing these complex systems. This method achieves the required computational complexity through a straightforward architecture: in each scale, it combines local pattern features with bottom-up features using a lightweight, bottom-up guided pattern extraction module, then feeds the resulting feature map into a point-based selection layer to isolate the most relevant features. However, Zhang et al. did not provide a computational complexity comparison against other approaches. This study reevaluates the complexity of the Zhang et al. network by estimating the number of floating-point operations (FLOPs) per inference, demonstrating that the original calculation was inaccurate because it overlooked the substantial computational load of convolution layers within the bottom-up feature extraction stages. Consequently, we propose a more precise complexity calculation method and provide a direct comparison with two recently proposed salient detection models. Based on this comparison, we introduce an even more accurate estimation approach for detection network complexity that accounts for the parameters of classifiers employed during inference. Our findings indicate that the Zhang et al. network is significantly less computationally efficient than two other models when both training and inference processes are considered. To the best of our knowledge, this paper offers the first complexity re-evaluation of the Zhang et al. salient detection network and proposes a more accurate calculation method. Additionally, we demonstrate that a more precise complexity estimation is essential for comparing the efficiency of different salient detection approaches. We hope this work aids future researchers in selecting models that best suit their specific application needs. In this study, we examine the percolation conditions for macroscopic bundles composed of chiral nanotubes, where particles are organized into concentric helical layers characterized by a specific helicity. Our findings reveal that percolation is facilitated in bundles containing fewer than three layers per particle, while it requires more than three layers to occur in bundles with larger numbers of layers. Additionally, the influence of particle thickness on conductance is analyzed. These results are derived from Monte Carlo simulations involving chiral nanotubes with varied helicity and thickness, deposited into bundles of predetermined sizes. To assess conductivity, we utilize two-point probe measurements alongside percolation theory. Finally, we discuss the implications of our Monte Carlo findings for experimental scenarios involving the growth of chiral nanotube bundles. Our research demonstrates that geometric factors play a critical role in achieving percolation and enhancing conductance in chiral nanotube materials. Consequently, these findings can guide the synthesis of materials with superior conductive properties. As a practical application, we illustrate how this mechanism can be leveraged to create electrical resistors and sensors with tunable sensitivity. Furthermore, we explore how to maximize the conductance of nanotube bundles for use in high-performance electronic devices. Ultimately, this work offers a pathway to significantly improve the conductivity of chiral nanotube assemblies. Additionally, we provide an analytical continuation of these results to a broader context, analyzing further geometric properties within the framework of percolation theory. This advancement enables the creation of novel functional devices utilizing nanotube geometric properties. Specifically, we analyze how percolation threshold, percolation paths, and average cluster sizes evolve within bundles of self-avoiding, chiral particles. The resulting materials exhibit unique properties that differ from those found in other assembly types. This analytical work serves as a foundation for future research into emergent phenomena in chiral nanomaterials. By integrating these findings with a newly developed percolation model, we can more accurately predict nanotube bundle conductivity and establish a solid basis for designing nanotube-based functional devices. This analytical approach also facilitates the investigation of phenomena that may be challenging to explore through simulations alone. Through this methodology, we gain deeper insights into the unique characteristics of chiral nanomaterials. Ultimately, these contributions provide essential tools for advancing future research in the field. We

This study investigates the quantum gravitational decay of superheavy dark matter (DM) to light fermions within the early Universe to establish new limits on DM interactions. Specifically, we focus on scenarios where the DM cross section scales inversely with a high power of energy, resulting in negligible production in the early Universe. Our findings refine existing bounds on various DM models, such as the Higgs portal, and suggest that these constraints could surpass current limits derived from direct detection experiments. Furthermore, this approach may constrain interactions with a future dark sector DM candidate. Finally, we demonstrate that our quantum gravity-induced bounds can complement, and in certain cases replace, those derived from early Universe overproduction problems. We conclude that imposing constraints based on DM interactions decaying due to quantum gravitational effects is a model-independent method for limiting the strength of interactions in dark matter candidates characterized by inverse power-law couplings. In contrast to the well-established search for dark photons using cosmic microwave background data, which is sensitive to qED breaking at the MeV scale, we demonstrate that quantum gravitational effects can restrict Higgs portal DM interactions at the TeV scale. Given that this DM scenario is a popular dark matter candidate, it is crucial to explore novel constraints beyond those arising from DM overproduction. Our work aims to stimulate further investigations into the implications of quantum gravity on DM interactions. In summary, we have demonstrated that in many scenarios, quantum gravity can significantly constrain the parameter space of popular dark matter models, potentially restricting Higgs portal DM interactions to values below 1 TeV. We have also provided an extensive discussion on the broader implications for other models. Ultimately, our study shows that quantum gravity can constrain the parameter space of various dark matter models, including the Higgs portal, in a model-independent manner. The SNR exhibits a double shell structure, with the inner shell spanning approximately 100 pc in diameter. FUV observations reveal a bright, elongated, and fragmented inner shell characterized by a complex morphology. This discrepancy suggests that the SNR is interacting with an inhomogeneous ambient medium, where the emitting material is pushed toward the direction of higher density. Furthermore, we identify a faint, rounder outer shell with a diameter of roughly 200 pc, which is also consistent with interaction with a denser surrounding medium. Finally, we calculated the age of SNR G106.3+3.3 to be approximately 10,000 years, based on the ratio of FUV to H-alpha emission. This type of explosion is particularly suited for creating the observed SNR morphology, as the abundance of Fe-56 in Type IIa supernova ejecta is significantly higher than in Type IIb ejecta. Furthermore, the transition from the inner to the outer shell may be attributed to the interaction between the SNR and the dense ambient medium. This study examines how information cascades evolve in dynamic networks formed by agents in social media who adopt new behaviors through a diffusion process. Specifically, agents transition to adopting new behaviors (e.g., opinions or trends) when a critical mass of their peers holds the same view. These agents form the internal network driving diffusion, while the broader network of followers outside these groups constitutes the external layer. We demonstrate that this dual-structure network amplifies cascades within agent communities and synchronously links them. Furthermore, we outline the characteristics of cascading sequences across both internal and external network levels. Finally, we show that agents within a community can collectively become influencers, facilitating cascades and aligning their adopters. Examining such nested, dynamic networks is vital for grasping the interaction between local and global processes during the diffusion of ideas, trends, and innovations. This framework offers a foundation for developing strategies to foster large-scale cascades and consensus within targeted communities. Keywords: cascades, dynamic networks, behavior diffusion, social media, influencers.

By applying this analysis to both power and energy efficiency metrics, the study demonstrates how to optimize the time-division multiplexing slot length in terms of duration. The efficiency gains from these techniques are subsequently quantified. Finally, the analysis is extended to distributed (irregular) links, revealing that the behavior of the memory term in this distributed environment differs substantially from the centralized case. Given the increasing relevance of optical amplification in optical networks, the work concludes by briefly discussing how to integrate an amplified section into the current framework. This integration results in a more complex expression for energy efficiency due to the presence of optical amplifiers. Nevertheless, the derived expressions remain applicable for calculating energy efficiency across various network scenarios, including both amplified and unamplified links, as well as power and energy efficiency in centralized and distributed configurations. In this new model, the temporal decrease of $\Lambda$ is directly linked to the formation of dark matter, thereby eliminating the need for separate dark matter and accretion terms in the acceleration equation. By fitting the model to Supernova Ia redshift and luminosity data, we derive the following values for the present-day universe: the dark energy parameter $\Lambda_0 = 1.2 \times 10^{-52} m^{-2}$, the matter parameter $\Omega_{m0} = 0.28$, the Hubble constant $H_0 = 67.74 km s^{-1}Mpc^{-1}$, the deceleration parameter $q_0 = -0.53$, and the dark matter density $\rho_{m0} = 2.6 \times 10^{-27} kg m^{-3}$. Additionally, the age of the universe is determined to be $13.79$ billion years. Furthermore, the transition from the deceleration to the acceleration phase occurs at a redshift $z_t = 0.77$, and the equation of state parameter for dark energy is calculated as $w = -0.95$. Finally, the graph of the deceleration parameter $q$ against redshift $z$ aligns well with observational data. The model's phase space representation also shows good agreement with observations. Ultimately, the age of the universe in this scenario is highly sensitive to the initial conditions. We conclude that the early universe required an extremely small $\Lambda$ value, whereas the current universe requires a very small $\Lambda$ as well. This implies that for the model to align with observations, the timescale for the evolution of $\Lambda$ must be extremely long. These findings may offer insights into the nature of dark energy. We determined the best-fitting model parameters for each disc by matching the model output to the ALMA visibilities. In total, we successfully fit 23 out of 27 observed discs using this methodology, with the four exceptions failing to converge due to significant short-scale structures in the ALMA images that the current model does not represent. Furthermore, we identified a significant correlation between the inferred turbulent viscosity and the gas-to-dust mass ratio derived from the ALMA observations. The goal is to determine cost-effective routing strategies for a fleet of vehicles to transport a group of riders using as few vehicles and cars per share as possible. Since rider locations and demands are unknown beforehand, they must be discovered during operation, leading to an online setting. Furthermore, new riders and requests may appear at any time, necessitating dynamic updates to the existing solution. Consequently, this work addresses online dynamic extended vehicle routing problems with uncertain demand. To tackle this, we introduce a novel online dynamic algorithm for extended ride-sharing (OND-ERS), which builds upon a new algorithm designed for certain demand scenarios. Extensive numerical experiments were conducted to evaluate this algorithm against others under various parameter conditions. The results demonstrate that OND-ERS performs robustly across different scenarios, particularly when demands fluctuate significantly. Additionally, we analyzed the impact of different planning intervals on computational performance. Our findings indicate that performance remains relatively stable across diverse interval settings. These outcomes highlight the substantial potential of on-demand and real-time decision-making in ride-sharing services. Overall, our experimental evidence suggests that on-demand and dynamic decision-making can be more efficient in terms of both cost and resources than relying on pre-planned routes and a static number of vehicles. Finally, a real-world case study was conducted in Barcelona, Spain, to empirically validate the approach. The deployment of OND-ERS in this case yielded positive outcomes regarding cost and resource efficiency. These results strongly suggest that on-demand and dynamic decision-making offers significant advantages over pre-planning, even in large-scale operations involving thousands of riders. To our knowledge, this is the first time an on-demand service has been applied to real-world dial-a-ride problems with uncertain demand. This model falls within the broader framework of non-autonomous non-linear Schrödinger equations, which often exhibit complex spectra and spectrally unstable configurations. However, we demonstrate that this specific equation possesses PT-symmetry and supports a family of time-periodic solutions on the anti-PT-symmetric subspace; these solutions serve as stationary states of an effective non-Hermitian Hamiltonian, whose non-Hermiticity stems from the coordinate-dependent nature of the non-linearity. Additionally, we identify a stability threshold in the spectrum that delineates regions of spectral stability and instability. Finally, the numerical results are interpreted by analyzing the stationary states and their associated anti-PT-symmetric linearized eigenfunctions. We conclude that the PT-symmetry and spectral stability of this equation can be understood through the properties of these stationary states and their linear eigenfunctions. This analysis underscores the utility of time-periodic stationary states and their linear eigenfunctions in clarifying the spectral properties of non-autonomous non-Hermitian Schrödinger equations. Furthermore, we note that the model is exactly solvable using the inverse scattering transform, which provides further insight into its spectral properties. However, deriving reliable estimates from published AI studies is difficult due to methodological flaws and incomplete reporting. To address this, we developed a framework to estimate generalization performance across diverse clinical settings and applied it to systematically analyze reported accuracy and model robustness in the diagnostic robustness benchmark (DRB). The DRB evaluates 13 state-of-the-art AI diagnostic models across seven medical imaging tasks, including breast cancer detection, lung nodule detection, and COPD classification. Our findings reveal that the models' generalization performance is substantially worse than standard evaluation metrics, with performance degrading by an average of 17% on the test sets of the DRB. These results suggest that the reported accuracy and utility of publicly available medical image diagnostic models may be significantly inflated, and that deploying such models in real-world clinical settings could face severe performance challenges. To ensure robustness, we advocate for external validation using a systematic search for domain shifts, which is more critical than achieving high accuracy on benchmark datasets. Furthermore, we propose that the AI research community establish community-wide external datasets to facilitate external validation and accelerate the development of clinically effective AI models. Finally, we outline a roadmap for creating such external datasets and emphasize the need for a more rigorous approach to external validation. This shift aims to reduce the gap between laboratory benchmarks and real-world clinical performance, ultimately leading to the development of clinically viable AI models. with the deployment of drone swarms offering a cost-effective, precise, and efficient approach to targeting. This research focuses on the self-organized control of such swarms. We propose a distributed control architecture that enables safe and efficient task execution within swarm missions. Specifically, this study investigates target acquisition using a ring formation of ten drones. To this end, we introduce the following innovations: (i) a distributed topological ring controller that maintains a circular formation around a target site while executing the mission; (ii) a time-varying, distributed assignment controller that orients the drones toward the target and minimizes both the total flight distance and energy consumption by optimizing the mapping between drones and the target; and (iii) a distributed path planner that generates collision-free trajectories for the oriented drones to reach the target. These proposed controllers are implemented using backstepping control, ensuring robustness against model uncertainties and external disturbances. The efficacy of the proposed distributed controllers is demonstrated through numerical simulations of ten drones acquiring a target from a distance of 100 meters. The simulation results indicate that the ring formation acquires a target within a distance of 10 meters in under 10 seconds, with all drones achieving synchronization. Furthermore, the formation maintains stability throughout the process, and the distributed path planner successfully avoids collisions. Compared to existing methods, our approach offers superior robustness against external disturbances, ensures distribution, and guarantees collision-free operation. This robustness is validated by the simulation outcomes, where the drones adjust their positions to mitigate the impact of distributed disturbances. Additionally, our method achieves faster convergence and higher accuracy in ring formation around the target distance. Finally, we show that the proposed approach not only reduces the time required to acquire the target but also significantly decreases the total flight distance and energy consumption by minimizing the deviation of the swarm from the target. These findings highlight the potential of our approach for military drone applications, particularly in automatically acquiring targets from long distances. In summary, the contributions of this paper are: (i) the development of a self-organized, distributed, and robust control method for swarms; (ii) the ability to acquire a target from long distances; (iii) collision avoidance; (iv) increased efficiency in target acquisition; (v) reduced time to acquire a target; (vi) minimized travel distance; (vii) lower energy consumption; and (viii) the achievement of all these objectives from a distributed control perspective. These distributed, self-organizing, and robust control strategies are essential for the autonomous acquisition of targets

Among these, the entropy of entanglement stands out as the most extensively studied metric, largely due to its operational clarity and direct link to resource allocation in pure-state quantum information protocols. Despite this significant theoretical progress, experimental efforts to calculate entanglement entropy have remained limited, with only a few studies achieving direct measurements of the entropy term itself. This paper reviews existing methods for experimentally determining entanglement entropy and presents a classification of these approaches based on the type of entanglement measure they assess. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive overview of recent advancements in this field. Through this survey, we demonstrate that the experimental landscape for calculating entanglement entropy has expanded rapidly in recent years, covering diverse platforms and techniques. We conclude by highlighting open challenges in this area and outlining potential future research directions. Recognizing that entanglement entropy serves as a key indicator of the complexity of correlated quantum systems, we argue that its determination remains a critical task for advancing our fundamental understanding of quantum many-body systems. Furthermore, we emphasize the significant role entanglement entropy plays in the recent emergence of quantum thermodynamics as a distinct research discipline. Specifically, we show that current protocols for extracting work from quantum resources fundamentally rely on the measurement of entanglement entropy. Additionally, we demonstrate that the entropy term in von Neumann entropy—defined as the von Neumann entropy of reduced density matrices—can be interpreted as a thermodynamic quantity representing the work extractable from a state's entanglement. This interpretation aligns with recent findings in quantum thermodynamics concerning the work potential of entangled states. Collectively, these findings underscore the fundamental importance of experimentally determining entanglement entropy. We believe this is essential not only for characterizing quantum correlations but also for advancing our understanding of thermodynamic processes within quantum systems. We anticipate that this perspective will inspire future experimental efforts to measure entanglement entropy across various quantum thermodynamic protocols. Finally, we demonstrate that the entropy term in von Neumann entropy can be measured with high precision across multiple quantum platforms, achieving a relative error of less than 1%. These results confirm that the rapid progress observed in measuring entanglement entropy using von Neumann entropy is supported by solid experimental foundations. By adopting this thermodynamic perspective, we aim to motivate future experimental investigations into the entropy term of von Neumann entropy. We demonstrate that this term holds thermodynamic significance and can be interpreted as quantifying the entanglement within a state. This thermodynamic interpretation of the entropy term

While conventional CD methods typically yield a single optimal path, we demonstrate that for a specific class of problems, multiple valid CD paths can be constructed from the same driving and auxiliary Hamiltonians. These alternative paths exhibit distinct properties, with the primary variation being in system entropy production; consequently, we can systematically tune this entropy by selecting different evolution paths. Given the prevalence of grayscale images and the need for accurate color-to-grayscale conversion, this study introduces a color to grayscale transformation utilizing the Inverse Ring Fourier Transform (IRFT). The IRFT involves two primary phases: first, image segmentation to identify the background color; second, color pixel classification by calculating the average R, G, and B values of each pixel to determine which channel is dominant. These R, G, and B determinations are executed in the frequency domain via IRFT to enhance robustness against pixel noise. Following the color identification, the image is converted to the RGB model, after which the two R, G, or B channels that are not dominant are discarded to yield the final grayscale image. Experimental results and the proposed evaluation metric confirm the method's high accuracy, with a 99.7% success rate in correctly identifying color pixels. The IRFT is particularly effective for color pixel identification within homogeneous images, even when contrasts are low. While the current implementation is image-specific, future work aims to extend this approach to similar images. Additionally, the method is computationally more efficient than alternatives, with a proposed computational complexity of O(n log n), where n represents the total number of pixels. Ultimately, a reliable, accurate, and efficient color to grayscale transformation is critical for enhancing image processing workflows. This paper presents the construction of GCM pairs over $\mathbb{Z}_6$ for any odd integer $m$ using Hadamard products, and provides an example for a pair over $\mathbb{Z}_4$ when $m=2$. Additionally, the concept of Bell-like games with exponentially quantized output advantages could find extensive application in areas such as randomness expansion, quantum computing, and quantum communication. Additionally, as an application of the concept of tabled agreement games, we apply them to a concept from category theory known as "weighted graphs," which can be interpreted as a generalization of finite graphs. Our findings indicate that, contrary to expectations, this diffusion does not converge to the continuous Schrödinger equation. Instead, it follows a hyperdiffusive pattern where the diffusion coefficient scales with the number of sites $N$ according to $N^{2+\alpha}$, with $\alpha$ taking values of $0$, $1$, or $2$. We elucidate the origin of these scaling behaviors and derive implications for a generalized discrete Dirac equation. Ultimately, we argue that this phenomenon is not unique to specific models but is instead an inherent characteristic of any non-relativistic field theory defined on a Euclidean discrete-time lattice. Consequently, the naive lattice approach is unsuitable for simulating non-relativistic quantum mechanics. Instead, we propose an alternative, fully relativistic method utilizing an ultra-relativistic fermion with mass $m$ approaching zero, where $m$ is measured in lattice units as $m = a m$. In this setup, the energy is given by $E = \sqrt{k^{2} + m^{2}} - |k| \approx m + \frac{1}{2}m$, thereby recovering the non-relativistic kinetic energy term $p^{2}/2m$. Numerical evidence confirms that a relativistic equation yields a diffusion process that properly converges to the Schrödinger equation in the continuum limit. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the ultra-relativistic limit of the Schwinger-Dyson equation produces the correct continuum propagator and interaction vertices for a non-relativistic gas of interacting particles. Additionally, we show that the ultra-relativistic model serves as an effective theory for a non-relativistic dilute gas, successfully reproducing the correct low-energy scattering amplitude and the correct scale-invariant wave function for two particles. Finally, we discuss the physical and computational implications of these results. In conclusion, we propose that the ultra-relativistic limit of the Schwinger-Dyson equation provides an efficient and reliable method for simulating non-relativistic quantum gases. This approach offers a novel and fully field-theoretic perspective on the relationship between the Schwinger-Dyson equation and quantum mechanics. This study investigates such chimera states within Ising networks, where each node represents an Ising-driven oscillator and interactions between nodes are defined by a directed adjacency matrix. We demonstrate the presence of both rotating and nonrotating chimeras in Ising networks, revealing distinct state-densities and the formation of connected components in the parameter space. We introduce a model system consisting of an autonomous agent that regulates its state based on past experiences, analyzing it through both dynamical systems and information-theoretic frameworks. By employing non-equilibrium thermodynamic methods, we demonstrate that the stationary distribution of this model is defined independently and interchangeably by either the agent's memory length or the quantity of data it stores. Furthermore, we utilize the concepts of work and entropy production to characterize and contrast our system with alternative dynamical models. This research offers a quantitative and thermodynamic understanding of how autonomous agents develop extended temporal correlations while maintaining short-term memory. The thermodynamic principles identified here may help explain the temporal structure of the longest-known fossils, spanning over half a billion years, as well as ancient geological and climatic data. These principles could also illuminate the temporal patterns observed in complex systems, extending beyond biology. Additionally, we propose that the total entropy production of a long-memory system can be measured by the mutual information linking the system's initial and final states. This finding provides a novel information-theoretic approach to examining long-term evolutionary trajectories, including those of living organisms and Earth itself. The model presented here is applicable in various domains, such as reinforcement learning and time series analysis. A Python package, "experienced agent," is available to facilitate the analysis of this model system. The thermodynamic arguments supporting our theory are robust, as they are corroborated by independent numerical simulations and analytical derivations. Our information-theoretic and thermodynamic characterization of extended temporal correlations offers a fresh perspective on diverse phenomena, ranging from the complexity of time series to the temporal structure of the geological record. This study aims to clarify various tunneling times, with a specific focus on dwell time and delay time. To build intuition, the classical scenario of tunneling through a narrow, flat barrier is examined, demonstrating that the ratio of delay time to group velocity accurately predicts traversal distance, whereas tunneling current remains independent of this ratio. In the quantum domain, these times generally scale with the barrier thickness $W$ as $W/v$, where $v$ represents the quantum velocity within the barrier. However, for extremely thin flat barriers, velocity becomes increasingly ambiguous, making both dwell and delay times uncertain and difficult to measure. Conversely, the quantum transmission phase shift, which also correlates with velocity and scales linearly with $W$, is demonstrated to be measurable using standard techniques in this thin-film regime. Additionally, it is shown that delay time does not align with the classical delay time under any conditions. Finally, the quantum system is modeled as a particle navigating a labyrinth of narrow tunnels, where tunneling occurs by connecting two adjacent tunnels via a narrow "bridge." In this configuration, tunneling time is determined by the bridge's width and remains independent of the vertical barrier height separating the tunnels. This model indicates that tunneling is effectively a two-dimensional process, and its success is validated by numerical calculations. The paper concludes by summarizing key insights regarding tunneling times and their implications. The arguments presented are designed to resolve longstanding controversies, including the question of whether tunneling is instantaneous. The primary focus is on simple scenarios, such as flat barriers and one-dimensional potentials, with the goal of extending these findings to more complex configurations in future work. The study demonstrates that various definitions of tunneling time can yield consistent physical results when applied correctly. For instance, tunneling times for a flat barrier are shown to be proportional to its thickness but not to the barrier height; this also applies to quantum transmission phase shifts, which can be interpreted as the time required to cross the barrier's thickness at a specific velocity corresponding to the transmitted energy. Furthermore, it is established that tunneling is not instantaneous, contradicting the often-cited but incorrectly applied classical argument suggesting otherwise. The analysis proves that this instantaneous traversal argument is only valid when a specific, inappropriate velocity is used to calculate traversal distance. Finally, it is demonstrated that tunneling is not a nonlocal process, as the delay time is accurately described by a model in which the particle's position is fixed at the entry point of the barrier

The ODEPACK solver was employed to solve the system of ordinary differential equations governing the spatiotemporal dynamics of temperature and salinity. To validate this approach, the model was applied to reproduce a paleoclimate record of temperature and salinity derived from the foraminifera *Neogloboquadrina dutertrei* in the Eastern Equatorial Pacific. Results indicate that the system accurately replicates the PETM and mdp-Pliocene events, capturing both the timing and magnitude of the observed data. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that PALEOCCENE effectively represents spatiotemporal dynamics in complex systems, even when dealing with sparse and irregularly spaced observations. This capability is achieved through a system of well-posed equations and a computational design optimized for both time-dependent modeling and data assimilation. The paper concludes by outlining future research directions. The source code is available at https://github.com/UCSD-AMOS/PaleoceneCE. This study presents the first theoretical assessment of the biased least-squares estimator's bias under the sky model. By employing a basis set of bandpass-beam convolved spherical harmonics, we extend existing bias results to a more realistic CMB map-making framework. Our findings indicate that, for all but the largest angular scales, the bias of the biased least-squares estimator is negligible. Furthermore, we demonstrate that on the largest angular scales, this bias is proportional to the bandpass beam width and is independent of the specific sky model. Consequently, the bias affects only the largest scales and can be effectively corrected through map mask relaxation. This theoretical understanding of the bias is crucial for accurately estimating the sigma eight (s8) parameter from CMB maps. We demonstrate that if this bias is not accounted for, systematic errors in s8 could reach approximately 0.03, with similar effects observed in other cosmological parameters. This conclusion holds for current and future CMB experiments, including Planck, Simons Observatory, and CMB-HD. Additionally, we show that properly accounting for the bias allows the cosmological parameter inference to achieve its full potential. In recent years, rapidly evolving fields like Information Retrieval (IR) and Social Network Analysis (SNA) have driven the creation of numerous centrality measures, each built upon distinct network properties and offering unique advantages and limitations. Despite this proliferation, no unified framework exists for comparing these measures within a specific application context, making it difficult to determine the most appropriate choice for a given task. This paper introduces a theoretical framework for comparing different types of centrality measures. Furthermore, we develop an application-oriented framework that establishes a topological structure for a specific measure based on its underlying network properties. This approach enables the identification of measures most suitable for a given application scenario. We determine the metric coefficients of block-diagonal form, where the off-diagonal element represents the classical frame-dragging effect. We demonstrate that this approximate metric, which is valid everywhere outside the rotating body, satisfies the Lineweaver and Minkowski-Papapetrou form for static, rotating axially symmetric metrics in empty spacetime and adheres to the first of Einstein's field equations. We show that the frame-dragging velocity field diverges near the surface of a rigidly rotating material body and argue that quantum field theory in curved spacetime must be employed to address vacuum polarization and the back-reaction of virtual particles on the classical geometry. Furthermore, we illustrate that this metric can be utilized to examine the Blandford-Znajek effect in the outer region of the space surrounding a black hole or a dark energy field under a slowly rotating approximation. In this context, we note that the angular velocity must remain finite and non-zero at the inner boundary of the region where the vacuum is quantized. Additionally, we examine the vacuum polarization effect and compute the leading-order correction to the Einstein-Hilbert action's beta function caused by the frame-dragging term. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for black hole mechanics and thermodynamics. By applying a variational principle to the effective metric that includes a quantum contribution from the rotating dark energy field, we derive the energy density of the dark energy field, its anisotropic stress tensor, and the cosmological constant. This approach yields the correct Hubble parameter, deceleration parameter, and the relationship between the black hole mass and its horizon radius, aligning with observational data. Ultimately, this study offers a viable alternative to the singular spacetime geometry typically assumed in standard black hole physics. Our findings suggest that the universe may contain an infinite number of black holes, with their collective effect on the cosmological redshift accounting for the observed dark energy. This offers a potential resolution to the black hole information paradox and provides an alternative explanation for the unobserved diffuse gravitational effect that would result from the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy of all black holes. While Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) utilize a latent space and a decoder, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) operate without a representation space but include both a generator and an inference network. In contrast to VAEs, GANs frequently produce higher-quality outputs, yet they are notorious for being difficult to train. We introduce GAEs as a unified framework that encompasses both VAEs and GANs, while also bridging other models like ScoreVAEs and Vector Quantized Variational Autoencoders (VQVAE-1). Furthermore, GAEs provide a more cohesive theoretical structure for addressing the challenges associated with training GANs. Specifically, they allow for quantitative assessment of how model components influence the stability and efficacy of GAN training, offering a more granular approach than traditional trial-and-error methods. This methodology is demonstrated using GAE-B, which combines elements of VAEs and GANs to generate more realistic images. Our results indicate that these models are easier to train than standard GANs and that the model complexity can be effectively managed to optimize performance. To validate this approach, we trained GAE-B on MNIST, FashionMNIST, and CIFAR10 datasets over approximately 100 epochs on an NVIDIA A100 GPU. The models achieved Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) scores of 2.87, 2.63, and 3.07, and Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) scores of 5.50, 5.04, and 5.54, respectively. These findings suggest that GAE-B produces superior images compared to pure GANs and is significantly easier to train. This work demonstrates the versatility of GAEs, as the models can be adapted across various domains, including medical imaging, where they offer particular advantages in terms of computational efficiency and accuracy. This paper examines the potential for pulsar timing array (PTA) data to detect neutrino GWs—hypothetical ripples in the spacetime interval caused by a relativistic flux of neutrinos—based on their unique spectral and timing characteristics. We outline the required flux flux and energy distribution for such signals to be distinguishable from gravitational GWs and the galactic rotation-induced "GPB" signal. Consequently, we propose that an optimal strategy to address the NPAsignal is to simultaneously search for gravitational GWs and neutrino GWs. If no gravitational GWs are found, the search for neutrino GWs can be used to establish upper limits on the galactic neutrino flux, with potential applications in astroparticle physics and neutrino physics. This approach represents a viable pathway for the next generation of PTA observatories. A positive detection would necessitate a re-evaluation of the Standard Model. (MO-MINLP) problems are prevalent in various engineering and industrial contexts, yet their intricate nature and the scarcity of efficient algorithms make solving them a challenging task. This study introduces a novel hybrid algorithm designed to tackle general MO-MINLP problems. The method integrates two distinct techniques: (i) a multi-agent system grounded in the Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) meta-heuristic for addressing Non-Linear Programming (NLP) components, and (ii) a Branch-and-Bound (BnB) framework applied to Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) sub-problems. This algorithmic framework utilizes two distinct objective functions: the first seeks to maximize the sum of objective function values while maintaining a feasible solution, and the second aims to identify a feasible solution that minimizes infeasibility penalties. The algorithm demonstrates efficacy across a broad spectrum of MO-MINLP problems, delivering high-quality outcomes even under tight computational time constraints. Furthermore, the experimentally derived Pareto fronts align exceptionally well with theoretical fronts across various test problems, indicating that the proposed method is capable of identifying all optimal solutions. Finally, the method's effectiveness is further validated by its superior performance compared to existing algorithms on a standard set of MO-MINLP test problems. These findings suggest that the proposed approach is well-suited to deliver competitive results in complex, real-world applications. Source Code: https://github.com/ahmed-elmahdy/DBNANDMOCA. Weakly-supervised learning serves as an effective strategy for training deep models using only coarsely labeled data. In the context of image classification, weakly-supervised learning typically involves training a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) based on images tagged with coarse categories, such as scene labels, rather than fine-grained annotations. This method has proven successful in various other fine-grained classification tasks, including bird classification, vehicle recognition, and food categorization. To facilitate further research in this area, we introduce the Cambridge Face Challenge (CFC) dataset, a new instance of the weakly-supervised learning problem. The CFC task requires learning to distinguish among 10 distinct face categories using training data marked solely with one of two coarse labels. We provide a detailed analysis of the dataset and its characteristics. To ensure a strong baseline, we present FaceNet, a state-of-the-art model trained for the CFC task that achieves 64.8% top-1 accuracy. Additionally, we establish a new state-of-the-art result of 81.1% top-1 accuracy through ensemble methods. To support future advancements, we release FaceNet, a state-of-the-art model trained via transfer learning from large-scale image recognition datasets. Our findings indicate that this approach is highly effective for weakly-supervised learning and can be readily adapted to other tasks. Code and data are accessible at: https://github.com/josephgao/WeakSupervisedLearning.

To model this process, we introduce a few-shot continual learning task that mimics human-like few-shot classification by requiring models to learn from merely tens of samples per class. Furthermore, the task's design ensures a difficulty progression where later classes are more challenging to handle than earlier ones. Our results demonstrate that current state-of-the-art methods fail in this setting, suffering from a performance drop of up to 40% on our hardest dataset. In response, we propose a dynamic vector similarity metric designed to address this difficulty bias. This metric adjusts the similarity function using a time-dependent weight for each dimension, enabling more accurate estimates of feature representation similarity. We show that incorporating this modified similarity metric into existing approaches yields significant improvements. Specifically, our experiments indicate that applying similarity dynamics to SimCLR results in a 14% relative gain, while applying it to a human-like data augmentation strategy improves performance by an additional 6% relative. These results represent a substantial improvement over current state-of-the-art methods. The efficacy of our similarity dynamics stems from its exploitation of meta-heuristics inherent in contrastive representation learning, which these methods implicitly develop over time. Consequently, our approach achieves a performance boost of up to 14% relative without requiring any task-specific modifications. We demonstrate that a vortex string can indeed form through nontrivial gauge symmetry breaking, even without local field vortices. In this configuration, the associated gauge field acquires a mass through the Higgs mechanism, resulting in a vortex string with mixed characteristics: it exhibits global string behavior at large radii where the field field follows a quasi-classical trajectory, while displaying local string properties at smaller radii. However, CPA also introduces intrinsic nonlinearities, including pulse temporal modulation caused by intrapulse cross-phase modulation (ICPM). Although ICPN is well-known for its impact on ultrashort pulses, its effects on nanosecond-scale pulses in the context of CPA have not been previously investigated. This study demonstrates the onset of ICPN in CPA systems using self-consistent nonlinear time-domain simulations. We track the temporal evolution of ICPN throughout the CPA process, observing oscillatory behavior even with mild nonlinear effects. This work represents the first investigation of the ICPN phenomenon within the widely utilized and versatile CPA framework. Furthermore, we address the underlying physical mechanisms, showing that the ICPN-induced temporal modulation can be interpreted as a standing modulation due to the interference of forward and backward traveling waves. This interpretation offers a means to suppress the effect by introducing specific chirps. Leveraging this insight, we successfully demonstrate the suppression of ICPN through numerical simulations. These strategies hold significant potential to enhance the performance of existing CPA systems and inform the development of future ones. Additionally, the proposed approach to understanding pulse temporal modulation may prove valuable in other fields where CPA is employed. In conclusion, this research serves as a crucial bridge between the domains of CPA and CPA-based laser-plasma acceleration. As CPA remains the primary method for generating the gigawatt-class pulses essential to the acceleration process, accurately predicting pulse temporal modulation via ICPN is vital for advancing this field. We anticipate that our insights will facilitate further advancements in this area. events. In 1927, Paul Dirac suggested that the cosmological microwave background could serve as a universal clock to measure cosmic time, a approach later adopted by cosmologists. This study examines the feasibility of using matter dark halos as a cosmic clock within the $\Lambda$CDM cosmological framework, focusing on their statistical properties. We analyze halo number density, mass function, and the time between successive halo formations across redshifts from 2 to 0, within a cosmological volume of $(100 \, \mathrm{Mpc}/h)^3$. Our findings indicate that while large-scale structures can function as a cosmic clock, their time distribution is highly irregular. For local structures, the virialization times are primarily governed by large initial density fluctuations. The resulting variations in the statistic $dN/d\log t$—representing the number density of halos virializing per unit time as time progresses—are significant, though they diminish at lower redshifts as the number of available trial volumes increases. Ultimately, we conclude that while dark halos can act as a cosmic clock, the irregularity in their formation times prevents them from serving as an effective time-keeping mechanism. Furthermore, this classical process of virialization in its early stages cannot be utilized for the same purpose. We also address the criticism regarding the impracticality of observing distant halos and demonstrate that this issue can be resolved by targeting halo cores rather than their surfaces. Additionally, we address the question of whether the virialization process itself can be treated as a cosmic clock, demonstrating that the answer remains negative. This work contributes to the understanding of alternative methods for measuring cosmic time. Our analysis relies on the \texttt{GADGET-4} cosmological simulation code, which generates the evolution of dark matter structures. The simulation volume yields approximately $1.5\times 10^6$ halos, with each dark matter particle possessing a mass of $10^6 \, M_{\odot}h^{-1}$. The simulation covers a time span of 20 billion years, spanning from $z=2$ to $z=0$. We define the formation time of a halo as the moment it first emerges. The simulation's numerical accuracy is estimated to be approximately 10 percent. We also explore the relationship between the virialization time of the most recently formed halo and prior large-scale structure formation. To address these needs, we introduce Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning guided by Adversarial Search (RLL-gabas). In this framework, reinforcement learning agents are guided by traditional adversarial search agents; however, whereas standard adversarial search assumes static opponents, our approach utilizes learning agents to simulate adversarial behaviors. This method builds upon the concept of adversarial minimax trees, which are constructed by backward induction to determine optimal moves by analyzing all possible future states. The primary innovation lies in representing these trees using a novel data structure called the adversarial minimax tensor. This tensor stores value estimates and policy information for every potential future state. Crucially, the tensor is not stored in full but is implicitly generated from a pre-trained model. This model functions similarly to a deep neural network but incorporates a new component: the adversarial search layer. This layer enables the integration of adversarial search principles into the network, allowing the simulation of future states. We demonstrate the proposed method through a real-world use case by implementing a cyber defense solution within an SDN environment. The simulation results indicate the model's efficiency in large state spaces and its resilience against both random and adversarial traffic. Subsequently, we establish that the two-point correlation functions for boundary primary operators align with those predicted by the dilute instanton gas of the ${\rm SYK}_d$ model. within a group setting, where feedback is provided at both the group and expert levels. The objective is to maximize the group's total reward while acknowledging that not all experts contribute positively to the group's decision. We introduce two new algorithms and prove that they achieve $\tilde O(1/\sqrt T)$ regret bounds relative to the best expert in a group of size $K$ over $T$ rounds, with regret defined as the difference between the sum of the best expert's rewards and the group's accumulated rewards.

Our initial algorithm operates under the assumption that the group provides the exact ranking of how much each chosen action contributes to the total reward. In contrast, a second, simpler algorithm requires only a sign of the contribution (positive or negative) rather than a full ranking.

Finally, our results demonstrate that simple, naive, or even randomized strategies cannot attain sublinear regret. Specifically, any algorithm facing a group of experts with sign feedback in each of $T$ rounds must incur regret of at least $\frac{T - 1}{2}$ against the best expert. Furthermore, we present an algorithm that achieves regret bounded by $\frac{T - 1}{2} + \frac{4(K-1)}{\sqrt{\pi^2}} \frac{\log T}{T}$, which is at most $\frac{3T}{2}$ for all $T \ge 1$ and $K \ge 2$. This approach utilizes a randomized strategy that selects each expert with probability $1/K$. To our knowledge, this represents the first established lower bound on group regret. Additionally, we provide an upper bound on this regret for the randomized algorithm, which is at most $\frac{3T}{2}$. These theoretical findings are supported by numerical experiments conducted in the context of medical diagnosis. In this scenario, a group of doctors diagnoses a patient based on a series of symptoms, with the true diagnosis hidden from all but one expert at the end of the game. Each expert may possess a unique diagnostic bias, and our goal is to determine a combination of expert diagnoses that maximizes the total reward. Our findings indicate that a randomized algorithm, which assigns equal probability to all experts, outperforms both naive and deterministic methods. This conclusion holds across various expert biases, including cases where the best expert is not always selected, experts contribute negatively to the total reward, and the number of experts exceeds the total number of possible symptoms. These randomized algorithms are particularly effective when a subset of experts provides negative contributions to the total diagnosis.

We develop a Dialectral Entropy (DE) loss function to regulate this distribution, thereby enhancing diversity within individual utterances. This paper demonstrates that any group $G$ exhibiting the Baer property and possessing a finite subgroup $N$ with the property that $N_1$ is normal in $N_0$ implies $[N_0:N_1]$ is finite, must itself be normal in $N_{-1}$. Furthermore, we provide a characterization of groups with the Baer property in terms of the independence subseries of their lower central series. Additionally, we establish that any torsion nilpotent group $G$ enjoys the Baer property precisely when $G/\Phi(G)$ is locally finite, where $\Phi(G)$ denotes the Frattini subgroup of $G$. Finally, we examine groups $G$ where, for any subgroups $N_1 \leq N_0$, the condition that $N_1$ is normal in $N_0$ necessitates that $[N_0:N_1]$ is finite; we term such groups as groups with the strong Baer property. It is well-known that finite groups always satisfy this property. We construct various classes of strong Baer groups, including some strong Baer $p$-groups of arbitrary finite rank. We also prove that any torsion nilpotent strong Baer group is locally finite and that a torsion nilpotent simple group is a strong Baer group. Consequently, any torsion simple nilpotent group is finite. Additionally, any torsion simple $E$-group is demonstrated to be a strong Baer group. Finally, we characterize strong Baer groups using the independence subseries of the lower central series. These findings are derived within the context of general group theory. interface conformal field theory (ICFT) have garnered significant interest recently due to their extensive algebraic and geometric characteristics, as well as their potential for modeling physical systems like topological defects in condensed matter and gauge/geometry dualities. This work demonstrates that both frameworks can be constructed using a unified method: conformal field theory on manifolds with boundaries or defects, defined by the equivariant cohomology linked to the volume form's Poincaré dual class. This specific definition yields a boundary operator and an anchor map, both of which are essential for formulating BCFT and ICFT. Furthermore, we will show that the equivariant cohomology itself functions as a key component in describing the global structure of these theories. To support this argument, we employ a specific model instance and apply an alternative computational method to equivariant cohomology, known as equivariant localization. Finally, we validate that this alternative approach is compatible with the equivariant cohomology definition by proving it aligns with the residue definition, which is particularly valuable for computing operator content in BCFT and ICFT. Collectively, these findings provide algebraic and geometric tools aimed at clarifying and advancing the study of BCFT and ICFT. This paper presents the initial performance analysis of an RIS-assisted wideband OFDM system by examining the impact of block-wise imperfect channel state information (CSI). To this end, we derive exact expressions for the second-order moment of achievable rates, which account for both imperfect CSI and Rician components, serving as a performance metric for practical deployments. Subsequently, we analyze the trade-off between the number of reflecting elements and block-wise CSI accuracy to identify optimal CSI acquisition intervals that ensure sufficient element counts to meet target performance goals. Furthermore, we investigate the performance benefits of RIS-assisted OFDM over conventional RAN-based OFDM by comparing their second-order moments under identical power and noise constraints. Finally, we evaluate the computational complexity of calculating these moments using discrete Fourier transforms, demonstrating that the proposed analytical approach offers substantial computational advantages over Monte-Carlo methods. Simulations validate the accuracy of our theoretical results. Notably, our findings indicate that second-order moment analysis is computationally feasible for outdoor wireless systems, where channel variations are rapid and CSI remains relatively stable over short intervals. However, this approach may be unsuitable for indoor systems characterized by highly dynamic environments and scarce spectrum resources. Additionally, we show that RIS-assisted OFDM offers minimal performance gain over RAN-based OFDM when CSI is perfect, but provides a significant advantage of approximately 10 dB when CSI is imperfect. These advantages diminish as the number of reflecting elements increases, necessitating a balance between second-order moments and the count of RIS elements. Most importantly, our results demonstrate that RIS-assisted OFDM can achieve the same performance with fewer reconfigurable elements, or alternatively, deliver superior performance with a higher element count. This analysis underscores the critical role of second-order moments in achieving optimal system performance. In summary, our study provides valuable insights for the practical design of second-order moment analysis, CSI estimation intervals, and the number of RIS elements. Future work should extend this analysis to multi-user scenarios, accounting for inter-user interference. Additionally, further research could explore second-order moments in the presence of hardware impairments, such as phase noise, offset frequency, and amplitude noise. Additionally, the impact of second-order moments on power allocation, beamforming, and user scheduling warrants investigation. Ultimately, these extensions will facilitate more accurate and efficient second-order moment analysis. In conclusion, this paper provides a comprehensive analysis of second-order moments for RIS-assisted OFDM systems, establishing a solid foundation for future research.

that identifies ACL2 representations of C constructs based on a homomorphism between the two languages. While the homomorphism for most C constructs maps directly to ACL2 representations within the code, certain constructs require additional coercion. The code handles ACL2 representations of both C constructs and programs, which are required to be well-formed according to a grammar defined in the system.

The authors developed this tool to accelerate the creation of C code verifying software implementations against precise ACL2 specifications. To support this workflow, they are also creating a proof engine for C that can leverage ACL2 proofs where feasible. As an initial step, the tool verifies that a subset of C is total, ensuring the absence of diverging infinite loops and undefined behavior, such as C pointer arithmetic on NULL.

Although the tool operates on standard C, its C code generator requires representations of C programs in ACL2. Consequently, the developers are simultaneously building a translator that converts C programs into ACL2 programs where C constructs map one-to-one with their formal representations. This formalization enables the tool to perform proofs within ACL2 and subsequently extract the proof steps to generate the corresponding C code. Furthermore, the process of generating this translator serves as a verification step to guarantee its correctness.

To facilitate correct code generation, the tool accepts ACL2 annotations on C code that specify the C counterparts of certain constructs, which the translator verifies to ensure consistency with the actual C code. Additionally, the process generates a C program that computes ACL2 representations of C programs; this program is then used to demonstrate the absence of dynamic memory allocation.

Finally, the paper outlines a process for proving the correctness of the C code generator within ACL2 to produce a verified tool. These efforts are part of the CProof initiative, which aims to develop verified proof rules and a verified proof engine for C using ACL2. Complementing this, the tool presented in this paper is a component of CCert, a project dedicated to creating a verified compiler for C within ACL2. Both projects are integral to the CProof ecosystem, which provides an extensive collection of C proof rules and programs designed to assist in constructing verified C programs using ACL2. Additionally, the paper details a model of C pointers and memory using ACL2, which serves as a core component of the verified C code generator. This model accurately represents C pointer semantics and is employed to verify pointer-related properties of C programs. The paper also provides a model of dynamic memory, demonstrating how a C program can verify the absence of dynamic memory usage in a given C program.

generalized Gauss-Newton (GGN) approximation is essential for algorithms utilizing a local model to train and interpret various machine learning methods. In deep learning, this local model is typically represented by the Hessian of the loss function, either directly or through low-rank approximations. For statistics, particularly for efficient hypothesis testing and outlier detection, the GGN matrix is frequently employed instead of the full Hessian. We introduce an efficient, model-based approach to measure and visualize the magnitude of a GGN matrix using its real eigenvalues. Furthermore, we present a multi-scale variant that facilitates the visualization of large-scale structures within the matrix. We apply this method to visualizing the behavior of GGNs across different machine learning and statistical modeling contexts. Notably, in examples where the GGN approximates the within-class covariance, our approach yields an interactive eigenvalue plot that serves as a class surrogate. In other scenarios, such as detecting outliers in regression, the method enables the visualization of distinct outlier structures at varying scales. Finally, we demonstrate how to visualize the specific contribution of a particular observation to the GGN matrix at multiple scales, a feature that is particularly valuable for model interpretation. All plots, including interactive and three-dimensional versions, are generated using the MNE-GGN software. Due to the method's computational efficiency, the resulting plots are quick to produce and suitable for integration into interactive visualizations. Given its interpretability and scalability, we believe this tool will be valuable for researchers working with large-scale GGN matrices. The code is available at https://github.com/koeppl/MNE-GGN.
